title: Transformers and Self-Attention
brief: Transformers ditched step-by-step reading so models could connect every word at once. Let's test your intuition on self-attention, positional tricks, and the memory walls behind long context.

questions.question: In plain words, what does self-attention let each token in a sentence do?
questions.answer: Self-attention lets every token look across the whole sentence and weigh which other words matter most. Each token then blends information from those relevant words to sharpen its meaning in context. That is how a model tells a river bank apart from a savings bank.
key_points: Each token weighs and pulls context from other relevant tokens in the sequence
Blending neighbor information updates each token's meaning to fit the sentence
questions.hint: Think about how you figure out who the word she refers to while reading a story.
questions.fun_fact: In a real Transformer, different attention heads split up the job, with some tracking grammar while others link pronouns to nouns.

questions.question: What two big advantages helped Transformers replace recurrent neural networks?
questions.answer: Transformers process all tokens in parallel instead of reading a sequence one word at a time. That parallelism makes training much faster on modern GPUs. They also link distant tokens directly in one step, so early context does not fade away.
key_points: Process all tokens in parallel instead of sequentially for much faster training
Connect distant tokens directly in one step without losing long-range context
questions.hint: Compare an assembly line moving one piece per beat against an open room where everyone talks at once.
questions.fun_fact: The original Transformer beat the world's best translation models after just three and a half days on eight GPUs.

questions.question: Why can raw self-attention not tell the difference between dog bites man and man bites dog?
questions.answer: Raw self-attention compares every pair of tokens symmetrically and has no built-in sense of word order. Without extra cues, shuffling a sentence gives the exact same attention scores. Models fix this with position signals, such as rotating queries and keys with rotary embeddings.
key_points: Self-attention compares all token pairs symmetrically and has no built-in awareness of word order
Models add positional encodings or rotary position embeddings so attention tracks position and distance
questions.hint: Imagine dumping puzzle pieces into a bowl and checking which ones match without looking at their spots.
questions.fun_fact: Rotary position embeddings rotate each query and key like hands on a clock so their dot product naturally reflects the gap between two words.

questions.question: In scaled dot-product attention, why do we divide query and key scores before applying softmax?
questions.answer: When query and key vectors have many dimensions, their dot products grow huge. Huge scores push softmax to extremes where one token takes almost all the weight. Gradients nearly vanish there, so dividing by the square root of the key dimension keeps learning alive.
key_points: Stop huge dot products from saturating softmax into flat extremes where gradients nearly vanish
Dot product size grows with vector dimension, so dividing by the square root of the key dimension keeps scores balanced
questions.hint: Think about what happens to a steep curve when you feed it gigantic numbers and try to measure its slope.
questions.fun_fact: With unit-spread inputs, a dot product's variance equals the vector length, so dividing by its square root snaps the spread right back to one.

questions.question: Why do decoder language models apply a causal mask during training instead of letting tokens attend everywhere?
questions.answer: During training, the model sees the entire sentence at once to stay parallel. Without a causal mask, each token would cheat by peeking at future words it must predict. The mask blocks all later positions, unlike bidirectional encoders that read both ways for understanding.
key_points: Stop each token from peeking at future words it is trying to predict during parallel training
Bidirectional encoders attend in both directions because they build understanding instead of predicting left to right
Future attention scores are set to negative infinity before softmax so their weights drop to zero
questions.hint: Picture taking a fill-in-the-blank exam while the full solution sits uncovered beside your desk.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to causal masking, one parallel pass over a thousand-word page trains the model on nearly a thousand separate next-word quizzes at once.

questions.question: How does FlashAttention run exact long-context attention much faster with far less memory?
questions.answer: Standard attention slows down by shuttling a giant quadratic score matrix to slow main memory. FlashAttention splits attention into small tiles that stay inside fast on-chip memory instead. It updates softmax block by block, avoiding slow memory traffic while keeping exact math.
key_points: Tile queries, keys, and values into small blocks inside fast on-chip memory without writing the full attention matrix to slow memory
Update softmax incrementally across tiles so the output stays mathematically exact
Standard attention hits a memory-bandwidth wall because the full score matrix grows quadratically with sequence length
questions.hint: Imagine cooking from ingredients right on your cutting board instead of walking back to a distant warehouse after every chop.
questions.fun_fact: FlashAttention actually does extra math by recomputing attention during training, yet finishes faster because slow memory transfers cost far more than arithmetic.

questions.question: During token-by-token generation, why does the key-value cache create a memory bottleneck, and how does grouped-query attention ease it?
questions.answer: For each new token, the chip must reload every past key and value from slow memory. Streaming that growing cache saturates memory bandwidth while the math cores sit mostly idle. Grouped-query attention lets several query heads share one key-value head, shrinking the cache to load.
key_points: Each new token reloads the entire stored key-value cache from memory, saturating memory bandwidth
Grouped-query attention shares one key and value head across multiple query heads to shrink the cache
Sharing heads keeps most of multi-head attention's quality while approaching single-head cache speeds
questions.hint: Picture hauling a giant filing cabinet to your desk for every word you type, then pooling one cabinet across teammates.
questions.fun_fact: In long conversations or busy servers, the saved key-value cache can easily grow larger than the model's own weights.

questions.question: Why did modern deep Transformers move layer normalization before each sublayer instead of after the residual addition?
questions.answer: Normalizing before each sublayer leaves the main residual path completely untouched from start to finish. Gradients travel straight down that clean highway without blowing up or fading in deep stacks. Putting normalization after the addition causes wild early gradients and needs delicate warmup schedules.
key_points: Keep an unbroken residual path for smooth gradient flow or keep early gradients stable in very deep networks
Post-norm puts normalization on the main path, causing large early gradients near the output and needing fragile warmup
questions.hint: Think of an express lane running directly through a tall tower with no toll booths slowing down the central line.
questions.fun_fact: Moving layer normalization before each sublayer lets deep Transformers train smoothly even without any learning-rate warmup at all.
